Can Kshama Sawant Build an Actual Socialist City in America? (The Nation)

Sawant has called the meeting alongside the Gender Justice League to discuss a spike in violence, particularly against transgender women, in the rapidly gentrifying, historically gay neighborhood. She is asking the audience to suggest “neighborhood-based solutions” that she can advocate for. She’s the Seattle City Council’s newest member, elected in November 2013, and the Council’s only socialist—in fact, the only declared socialist in the legislature of a major US city.

The crowd includes young gay, lesbian, and transgender people who live on the street, middle-aged career activists, and even Seattle’s mayor, Ed Murray, who briefly takes the podium to talk of his own activist history in that very church and neighborhood. Mostly, though, the elected officials listen as a group of activists speak. It quickly becomes clear that this event will not call for increased policing and stronger hate-crime laws; instead, speakers point out that hate violence often comes from the police.

Ms. Sawant has proved to Seattle that she has her heart in the right place, and that she knows how to listen to her constituents. She met with representatives from some of the most marginalized groups in Seattle, and heard their grievances and suggestions. But can she take action? Is there even any action she can take to drastically improve the conditions of queer people and homeless people in Capitol Hill? They all seem to agree that more police patrols will not help to curb violence against queer people. Many times, the police are the ones bullying and beating trans women and others.

So what is the solution? Rent control will help give the disadvantaged a place to live, but what we need to really transform the culture of heterosexism and violence against queer people is complete social revolution. Can Ms. Sawant help forward this revolution from her position of authority? Or does her presence on the city council simply serve as a release valve, to reduce and assuage the righteous anger and indignation of the queer, the homeless, and the underpaid?
I really hope she succeeds. What a beautiful vision.
